utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian assisted by Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic assisted by Danilo Cirkovic as case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we start immediately with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Beglerbegovic. My name is Branko Lukic. And together with Mr. John Ostojic, I represent the Defence of Dr. Milomir Stakic before this Tribunal. Yesterday, you answered the questions of the Prosecution. So I would like to ask you to please help us today to clarify a number of points. First of all, when you spoke about the meeting you had with Mr. Stakic in 1996, what purpose was this meeting held for, can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was organised by an international organisation. I can't remember whether it was the OAC, or which organisation. They wanted to establish some sort of a contact between the Prijedor Merhamet and the Red Cross for Republika Srpska, or more precisely, the Prijedor branch of the Red Cross. At this meeting, we spoke about the then forthcoming elections. We discussed some figures, how many people were expected to vote, but not that I can remember too many details from the meeting right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also spoke about the founding of the party founded by the Belgrade lawyer Veljko Guberina and whose member Dr. Milomir Stakic also became in Omarska. Do you know that this party had a common list for the elections with the SDS for the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know this, and I did not know that the lawyer Guberina was involved. I knew that there was a gentleman called Guberina involved and he was quite famous in the former Yugoslavia, but I didn't know anything about the common list with the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As even before the conflict you had lived in Prijedor, do you know anything about the conflicts within the SDS, or anything about the different factions within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I know nothing about this. I was not in a position to learn anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Dr. Stakic was fired from the position of the president of the municipality in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was fired, but I don't know the reasons. I know that he was replaced by a man called Kurnoga.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember -- I'm not saying that you should remember, but if you would just try to remember -- after the takeover on the 16th of May, there was a festive assembly of Prijedor municipality, some Bosniak intellectuals took part, too?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I do remember that the 16th of May was a holiday in Prijedor municipality, the liberation of Prijedor. But the meeting you are talking about on the 16th of May and any Bosniak intellectuals taking part, frankly, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know of the existence of a crisis staff of the Party for Democratic Action as opposed to the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that. And I was not a member of the SDA. From my position then, I did not know anything about any such staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know of the existence of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Democratic Party as distinct from the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't realise that there were two different Crisis Staffs there, that those were two distinct Crisis Staffs. I only know that there was the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality, and all the members of that Crisis Staff were also members of the SDS, at least as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about a number of those. It's difficult to say now because on Prijedor radio, there were certain appeals and certain proclamations always on behalf of the Crisis Staff. But whether I have seen any of those, I was told by people who had been dismissed that their dismissal was on the behalf of the Crisis Staff. But I never had an opportunity to actually myself look at any such decision. I never held any of these in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please help us with the following: What did these proclamations relate to, excepting the issue of turning in weapons as you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a number of operational issues, some suggestions were is made, some solutions were proposed. And in the intervals between such messages, there were pamphlets. That's what I called them. Flinging mud at certain Muslims, well-respected citizens. So the intention was to paint them as extremists to the citizens of Prijedor. So, for example, a man who was working in the secretariat of national defence, a man named Becir Medunjanin, a teacher from Kozarac, the statements made on the radio, they didn't call him Medunjanin, but rather "Medunjani", which was supposed to be associated with some sort of Albanian ethnic origin purportedly. Ganic, Ejup Ganic they didn't call him Ganic, they called him "Ganici", which was supposed to connote something even more antagonistic to the Serbs. So by adding these different overtones to their family names, the aim was to emphasise animosity or hostility towards the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the Crisis Staff behind these pamphlets?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote these pamphlets, but I know that many things were done on behalf of the Crisis Staff. But I couldn't say for sure whether these pamphlets were written by the Crisis Staff. But it all came from the same frequency, from the same radio station. First the message, the announcement by the Crisis Staff, and then immediately following the announcement, this sort of message.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that after the takeover, you worked for a while but that you were IDed on the way to your work, to the hospital. Was everyone IDed at the checkpoints? Before people were IDed, could you tell who they were?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of checkpoints. If you mean at the hospital reception, everyone was IDed there. But, for example, the checkpoint at the crossroads, it very much depended on who was manning the checkpoint, whether he knew the person approaching or not. So I allow for the possibility that there were certain people who were not IDed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just remind the witness to pause briefly before answering the question because we need to hear the translation before he begins his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Beglerbegovic, it might seem a bit unnatural. We're used to reacting immediately.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also said and explained that quite many Muslims and Croats could not go to work because roads were blocked and checkpoints had been set up along the roads. However, is there any legal possibility to fail to report to work for six days in a row without being dismissed? You were the head of a unit at the hospital, so you must know about the -- you must know about the legal provisions in such cases.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason those persons failed to report to work were not only the checkpoints, but there was no public transport, no bus lines, no railway lines. Everything simply stopped. People couldn't even use their own cars, perhaps due to the checkpoints. But those who commuted to work by bus or by train could not come because there were no means of public transportation. It had all stopped. Whether this was unjustified, if you're only talking about six days of failure to report to work, but if for six days there were objective reasons that these people could not, were not able to, come to work, I think it is very questionable if this can be seen as a justified excuse to dismiss someone from their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned Dr. Radojka Elenkov. Do you know which ethnic group she belonged to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, she was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Isn't Elenkov actually a Bulgarian surname?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this was actually her husband's family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your wife work in Prijedor after the 30th of April, 1992? And then on until 1995?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she did. She worked in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us what sort of work she had?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you mentioned the 30th of April, that was the time of the takeover in Prijedor. She worked throughout the whole of April. That is, until the end of April. Hold on, just can I have a minute to try to remember. Yes, she worked until the very end of April. And then when the takeover took place, she no longer worked. But what you're probably Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. aiming at, what you probably want to get at, until 1990 [as interpreted], she worked in a private pharmacy privately owned by a man name Mihajlo Bundic [phoen] who was, by profession, a car mechanic or a driver, something like that. Under the circumstances, he found it convenient to open a pharmacy. And in order to open a pharmacy, there had to be someone qualified involved, and my wife was unemployed at that time. He practically forced her to take up the job. It was not of her own free will. There were a number of ugly scenes there. Unfortunately, this man is no longer around. But at the time he was so arrogant, we take off our shoes when we enter a house. That's our custom. And he walked into a house with military boots on with a grenade at his belt and a pistol. He laid his pistol on the table and began to talk. So one of the reasons he gave for her to start work, she was telling him that she didn't feel like doing that sort of job. It was a difficult job. She didn't want to leave the house. But then he said: "The Turks -- the Turks were torturing us for 500 years, but now it's time for us to get back on you, and now you will have to work for me." He was sitting at the window. He looked across the road, and he said: "This house is not really much of a house, because I can throw a hand grenade here or that window there." The suggestion was basically if she turned down the offer, the job offer, he wanted to show us what would happen to us. So that was a very ugly episode, and she was forced, basically, to work for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your wife receive a salary for her work?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she did, except when the last salary was due, but probably the owner of the pharmacy knew that we would be expelled, he kept the salary back, and we were expelled. She was supposed to get her salary on the 1st of October, so he never paid this salary to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said yesterday something about your obligation to report to work during the time you spent on standby. Were the Serbs, who had been put on standby, also obliged to report to their companies at certain intervals?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you had failed to report to the hospital, would you have been arrested for that reason, or did you only continue to report to the hospital only to keep your rights?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I would have been arrested. That was not a prescription really. I had to report to work to keep my place there, because whoever did not fail to report to work, his employment did not continue but at least he stayed there. So between two reports to work, many people left Prijedor in different ways. So a failure to report very often meant that a person had left Prijedor, and he was automatically eliminated from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can the Registrar please show Dr. Beglerbegovic yesterday's evidence, exhibits, bearing the numbers 124B and 125B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you can see what we are talking about. You saw these documents yesterday. Was yesterday the first time you laid eyes on these documents?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The names in the documents, but I knew about the existence of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Both these decisions, if you will agree, talk about interns, about specialist trainees?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that -- whether Mirsad Osmanovic and Miss or Mrs., Dr. Majda Sadikovic, do you know if they were in Prijedor at that time, or were they outside Prijedor somewhere, taking courses?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find that very difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you can tell us, it's all right. If not, not.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that also Serb employees who failed to report to the work obligation were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to go back to the 30th of May, the day of the attack on Prijedor. You told us that you had no time on that day to turn in the weapons that you -- that were legally in your possession, as you meant to. You only mentioned that a soldier walked into your house, took the gun, and left. Were you arrested on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. They only walked into my house, not one soldier but rather two or three soldiers. They passed through my house. They had a look. They didn't really search the house, but no, I was not arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The question, the previous question, I'm sorry I should have objected earlier, I believed, and I could be incorrect, he incorrectly stated the witness's answer from yesterday. I don't think he said the gun was taken during the search, but that he -- I don't want to lead the witness. I believe he explained yesterday what happened with the gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's easy, for the reason that we have a transcript. Could the Defence counsel please tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Page 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Page 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I will read this in English now so you get a proper and accurate translation. [In English] "So I didn't turn it in where I was supposed to turn it in, but it was taken from me with no written certificate. One of the soldiers just took it and left." [Interpretation] Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you or any of your relatives maltreated on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one was maltreated. The group that was staying close to my house at a checkpoint, they were the people who came in and took the gun. Aside from the gun, they only took the battery for my car because there was a car that they weren't able to start. So they took the battery from me, but there was no physical maltreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same day, the day of the attack on Prijedor, you said that the attack appeared to have somewhere from the direction of the bridge on the Sana. Is Stari Grad too in the same direction?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From where I live, yes, it is the same direction, Stari Grad and the bridge. Perhaps 2 or 300 metres distance, perhaps not even that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about announcements on the radio, announcements that were released after the attack on the 30th of May, 1992. On page 27, line 1, you state: [In English] "They explained they extorted. And one such announcement that got me really worried at that moment was an announcement requesting all the citizens of Prijedor to recognise the authorities. But they said at the end of the announcement that the safety of the Muslims was not guaranteed." [Interpretation] In connection with this announcement, I would like to ask you the following question: After this announcement, that is, immediately after this announcement, did anyone come over to your house to kill you, maltreat you, or beat you? Did your family suffer any consequences of this announcement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same night, or the night after the announcement, there was no one. I barricaded myself inside my house as best I could, in case anyone tried to break into the house. However, after several days, perhaps four or five days, a man from the group, the group who had come to my house and taken the battery from my car, met me in the garden outside my house and told me: "Doctor, you've done pretty well so far, haven't you? My people wanted to kill you, but I wouldn't let them. You should get 500 deutschmarks ready for me. I'll be back in 15 minutes. If you don't, they will be back tonight, and you will meet a very cruel fate." Before he told me this, the reason he had given was he was asking whether I had an aspirin for a friend of his who had problems urinating, and I knew the man. I went back to the house. I brought some medicine, and I tried to help him. And as I was searching in my bag for the medicine he had requested, he told me what I have just said. And then he left. I was dead scared. And clearly, I was not in a position to wait for him. In my neighbourhood, there was a checkpoint. I went to the checkpoint, and I reported this incident there. My Serb neighbours were at the checkpoint. They knew me. They came to my garden, and they waited for him. And eventually he came. They caught him and took him to the garrison. There was -- I'm not sure whether that was for a military purpose because he, too, was wearing a uniform. So they didn't take him to the civilian police station, but to the garrison on Urije. And according to the accounts of those who had taken him, they beat him there, and they even took his TV set. They came to me to ask me whether it was my TV set, and I said it wasn't. But due to the intervention of the people who were manning the checkpoint, unfortunately he didn't do anything bad to me. I was afraid afterwards that they would release him from the garrison where he had been taken. But fortunately, he never showed up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke yesterday about the white flags and blankets that Bosniaks and Muslims were ordered to put up outside their houses. Did people obey this instruction? Did they put up these flags and blankets?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did that last for, these flags and blankets? Were they removed later?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, approximately how long this lasted, the flags and blankets outside the houses?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say with any degree of precision, but for about four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spoke about your stay in Omarska. I mean, the camp, not -- I'm not referring to the time you worked there as a doctor. You said you were put in the glass house. Can you tell us about the makeup of the people who were in the glass house?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already said this yesterday. Those were people who were different in some way, whether they were wealthy people, well-respected people, or perhaps some had, like me, someone they knew who gave them this privilege to be in the glass house. As I said, the conditions in the glass house were much superior to those in any other facilities in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that you were brought to Omarska rather late, but I will try to ask you something about the beginning of the functioning of this camp, in case you heard about it from other people. Do you know that for the first ten days or so, a lot of the people who were interrogated were released from Omarska, about 70 people a day? Did you hear something like that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I even saw those people. A large number of people -- of those people were from the village of Puharska, and they had to pass by my house on their way back to the village, and that's when I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you managed to have your brother moved to the glass house, that you were afraid for him because he was exposed to view there. Do you know whether the -- he was ever called out or maltreated because of the fact that he had been put into the glass house?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. However, at that moment, going there, as I said yesterday, was a wrong move. But fortunately, our fears were not realised, and he did not have any negative consequences because he was moved there. It never happened that they called out his name because he was there, but of course the same thing happened to him as happened to everybody else who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your brother leave Omarska alive?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my brother is still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were released from Omarska, and you explained how this came about, you said that they would not let the people, the Serbs from the village of Omarska take you away, but that they insisted you be taken back in an official vehicle together with the inspectors from Prijedor. You then explained that on that day, you did not get a certificate that you had been released, but on the following day, you again went to the SUP, that is, to the police, and that Simo Drljaca issued this certificate for you. Did Simo Drljaca ask permission from anyone to issue you with this certificate, or did he do this in front of you, without consulting anyone else?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he asked anyone, but I didn't see that during the time I was in his office. I didn't see him contact anyone or ask anyone anything, so I can't tell you whether this happened or not. But it was he who issued the certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. On your release from the camp of Omarska, did you return to your flat or house -- forgive me, I'm not sure what sort of housing you had. But did you go back to the same housing you had before?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my own house where I live, and yes, I did go back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the Serbs were looking for excuses to start a conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we have just for the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sure, that's page 67, row 21, Your Honour, yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I will read this again to you in English. [In English] "They were looking for excuses to start a conflict. Some sort of attacks were mounted. A scenario was created in several places, and all this leads me to conclude that none of it happened by chance." [Interpretation] When you say that "none of this happened by chance," do you mean the incident at Hambarine on the 22nd of April, the attack on the military column on the 24th of April in Kozarac -- I apologise, it was the 24th of May -- and also in the case of Hambarine, it was the 22nd of May --, and the 30th of May, the attack on Prijedor, or were you referring to something else?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned three events, Hambarine, Kozarac. I know very little about those. But I heard the official version that was broadcast over the radio, that is, the Serbian version, one might say with some reservations, of these events. But I have to explain what I mean. Dr. Esad, known as Eso, Sadikovic, just before the conflict in Prijedor spent a lot of time with a military centre Radmilo Zeljaja, I don't know what his rank was, and with someone else who was perhaps a colonel. I'm not sure about the rank. His name was Arsic. The two of them were members of the JNA which was already, I think, the Army of Republika Srpska, although I'm not sure about all these dates. I may get confused about the dates, so please forgive me if I do. It's not my strong point, remembering dates. But Zeljaja and Eso went around town together. They sat in cafes. They kept company. And there were some initiatives to prevent the conflict because the conflict was in the air. It was imminent, and Eso was a man who had authority, not only among the Muslims. He was well-respected. He was a well-known citizen. He used to write articles in the newspapers, the Kozarski Vjesnik, and he had -- well, it wasn't exactly a column, but something of that sort. And people would wait for Friday in order to buy the Kozarski Vjesnik to read Eso's articles. So I'm telling you all this to show you what sort of man this was, how well-respected he was. And I am sure that Eso wanted to do this. On one occasion, he told me that Ratko Mladic had called Zeljaja on the telephone and had cursed him, used the foul language, and said: "What are you waiting for? Why don't you begin?" This is what leads me to conclude they were looking for an incident, for an excuse, to begin. Because I do not believe that Eso would have told me this if he hadn't been told by Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you again. I do allow for the fact that you don't know. But did you hear that the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina issued an order to attack facilities and columns of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In April, May, June, was the area then known as the Autonomous Region of Krajina cut off from the other parts under the control of Serbian forces, and do you know that in order to connect the Autonomous Region of Krajina with Yugoslavia, there was fighting in Posavina in order to create a corridor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the period when this happened, but I know there was a time when it was cut off and that there was fighting to establish a corridor. But I wouldn't be able to tell you when this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether people left Prijedor before the takeover of power on the 30th of April? Do you know that there were buses going to Croatia and to western countries?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People did leave. I wouldn't say there were buses taking people to Croatia. I think many of them used the air transport to Belgrade because very quickly the bridges over the River Sava were destroyed. So I think there was no communication, although I'm not sure. But since you ask me, I remember people leaving by plane more than by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you were unable to move around during the curfew, do you know who was able to move around during the curfew? If you don't know --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. According to the rules, then it's quite clear who has the right and who did you not have the right to move around during the curfew. But who actually did move around, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear Dr. Stakic holding any sort of speech before the Serbs took over power in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just remind you of some things you said in your statement of the 13th of January, 1992, and then I will ask you to comment. On page 1 of the B/C/S version -- in fact, it's page 4524, the last paragraph, you say: "All through the crisis years of 1990, 1991, and 1992, SDS claimed to represent all Serbs in Bosnia. The Prijedor branch of SDS made the same claim with respect to the Serbs in Prijedor municipality." First of all, can you explain to us why in all three years, 1990, 1991, and 1992, in your opinion, why all these three years were crisis years?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I said "crisis years." It's possible. If that's what it says, then I did. But they were crisis years because they preceded the events that followed. So they must have crisis years because they led up to the war and everything that happened. And the SDS was the most numerous Serbian party, the best represented after the elections. Its members found themselves in elected positions, and of course they were in a position to carry out and implement the policy of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the same time, the SDA and the HDZ also claimed to be the only legitimate representatives of their respective ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, although there were other parties, but it's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possible. They did make that claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 4525 of the same statement, you say, commenting your previous statement made to the Tribunal investigators: "In my last statement, I said that in a way, SDS became the most powerful factor in the municipality, more than the president of the municipality. The most obvious persons who represented the SDS were Srdjo Srdic and Simo Miskovic." What led you to this conclusion, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... In the English version, it's page 3, entire paragraph 4. Paragraph 4, entire paragraph 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concluded this because they were at the head of the party one after the other. They spoke most often in the media on behalf of the party. And it was from their mouths that I heard words that were later implemented and put into practice. That's why I mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, we are reaching the end of your cross-examination. I will ask you for just a little more patience. I would like to mention some names to you. You know these people. I would like to ask you only whether you know what they are doing today, whether they are alive and whether you know anything about their fate today. You lived during the war in Prijedor. Do you know whether Mr. Alicehajic, Satko, also lived in Prijedor during the car?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cehajic? Alicehajic, Alicehajic, Sead, Satko, who was a car electrician, a panel beater. He lived in Prijedor throughout the war and he still lives there, yes. If necessary, his wife's sister, his sister-in-law, is married to Srdjo Srdic's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Mr. Alicehajic a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sead Alajbegovic, tradesman, do you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he live in Prijedor throughout the war and does he still live there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he did, and he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sead Pesic [as interpreted], he was the chief of the public security centre station in Prijedor, and later on in Banja Luka. Do you know where he is?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. His name is Besic, Sead Besic. He is still in Prijedor. He spent some time in Banja Luka during the war. He was hiding. He wasn't in Prijedor. It could have been between 1993 and 1995, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure. All I know is that he was not in Prijedor for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alajbegovic and Besic, are they Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Dinka Tatarevic, a journalist?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know her, too. Her married name is Kovacevic. Tatarevic is her maiden name. Kovacevic, her husband is a Serb, and he is related to Mico Kovacevic. And Mr. Alajbegovic and Mr. Besic are both in mixed marriages with wives who are of Serbian nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Senija Dzafic, an announcer on Radio Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know she was there, and she was there throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Fatima Karagic, a teacher?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Iso Bucan. Before the war, he was a chief in the defence department?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Iso.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is he in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Azra Hajdukovic, a secondary school teacher?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She is married to Ziko Hajdukovic, a secondary school teacher, who is a Serb by nationality. Yes, she is in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Edin Susic, another secondary school teacher?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him, too. He is also in a mixed marriage, and his wife is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ismet Katardzic, a teacher?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the same case as before. He is in Prijedor, and he's married to a wife who is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I won't trouble you any further. Thank you. Thank you very much for answering our questions also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The trial stands adjourned until 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I now ask for the questions of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I just have a few questions to clarify what you told us this afternoon. You talked about Dr. Sadikovic telling you that he met with Zeljaja to discuss avoidance of the conflict and that Zeljaja told him that he had received instructions or some comment from Ratko Mladic "what are you waiting for," that Mladic had said that to Zeljaja. When you talked about Ratko Mladic, is that General Ratko Mladic who became the commander of the VRS, the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I was talking about that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Second area is: You talked about an incident where a soldier demanded from you 500 deutschmark or indicated that something could happen to you if you didn't pay 500 deutschmark and that your neighbours took this man to the military barracks. Did any investigators from the police or military ever interview you about this incident?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, you mentioned an incident with your wife or the fact that she had been asked to work for a man who came to your house with a grenade -- I don't want to repeat everything that you said. But it was not clear to me when that incident occurred. Can you tell us in what year, and if you know, what month approximately that incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been in the autumn of 1994, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, the Judges have some questions. In answering a question of the Defence this afternoon, you mentioned that Dr. Stakic was fired October 1992 and replaced by Mr. Kurnova [sic]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that Dr. Stakic was not the president of the municipality for a while. I don't know the exact period, but I'll allow that what the Defence said was true. And I know that he replaced Mr. Kurni [as interpreted] as the president. That was the man's last name. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: He replaced or he was replaced by?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I could tell anything about the circumstances under which this occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be quite clear, Dr. Stakic was replaced by this Mr. Kurnova [sic]. Is this correct, in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just, the Witness has indicated he's not sure of the date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not a question of date. It's a question of who was replaced by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Because on the transcript, you can read the contrary.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kurnova [as interpreted] came to replace Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. But you don't know anything about the details. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not know anything about the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yesterday, in your statement on the transcript in English page 38, you said the following, I quote in context: "The next day when I got up in the morning, I was in the glass house. I saw Zeljko Meakic, who was the commander of the camp. He was wearing a uniform and he gave a sign, beckoned me through the glass to come out, and then I came out. And he said: 'I have good news for you. It is 98 per cent certain that you will be released and go home. And as for the 2 per cent of uncertainty, wait until I come back from Prijedor,' which means that he had been told that I was to be released but he had to go to Prijedor to double check. So that's how he explained the situation to me." From page 38. And then on page 43, you continued, line 4: "Yes. When Meakic arrived with his news from Prijedor that a definite decision had been reached to release me, the word went around and a group of people from Omarska who were not guards but simply residents of Omarska who knew me from before I arrived in the camp wishing to take me away because the news spread very quickly through the village, through the neighbourhood." Did you discuss with Mr. Meakic or did you learn by chance why he had to go to Prijedor and with whom he spoke in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk to him about this. He didn't tell me anything, and that is simply what the situation was like. Excuse me. I was happy to be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. released, and I was interested in nothing further. And he didn't tell me anything. So I really couldn't say who he talked to, who he went to consult, and who issued the approval for my release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is undoubtedly your testimony that you say he went to Prijedor and came back telling you that the decision was taken, and therefore you were released?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the moment -- between the moment he told me he would go to Prijedor and the moment he told me a decision had been reached, there may have been three or four hours in between. I never saw him get into a car or go to Prijedor or return from Prijedor. But that's the time that elapsed between the moment he told me the one thing, and then the other thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you remember very well that he said, and it is in the transcript in quotation marks, that: "As for the 2 per cent of uncertainty, wait until I come back from Prijedor." This is right? This is your memory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's now turn to your statement you gave the 13th of January, 2002. One can find on the cover page that the languages used in the interview were English and Bosnian. One can find under the English version your signature. Did you read this document in the English version, and could you understand this in the English version?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was read out to me in Bosnian language. My understanding of English is quite poor. I don't speak English. I understand some English. But I don't think I can have been able to read a text like this in English. But the text was translated to me, interpreted to me, consecutively, and then I signed the statement. The interpreter was interpreting my statement to the investigator, so I had every confidence that what the interpreter said was true and correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, please, allow me that we really can be sure that what is laid down in this document is your testimony also today, to read out several paragraphs of this document. And I will do it slowly and stop after each sentence. And in case you have to add something or something might be wrong, please intervene immediately. On page 3, the English version, full paragraph 4, taking into account that full paragraph 3 was already read out by the Defence, I quote, and then sentence by sentence: "I would like to point out that following the takeover, there were no conflicts between the president of the municipality and the SDS."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't state this with certainty. I mean, that I really did state this. I was not in a position to know whether there were any conflicts or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question is not whether or not -- of course, this is a point of departure whether or not you can identify a discrepancy between this document and that what you really know. But you will understand that what we are interested in is what you really experienced at that time in 1992. And therefore, as you did it here, please add your comments to these single sentences. To continue: "They were acting as one and the same. Milomir Stakic, in his capacity as president of the municipality, implemented the plan of the SDS."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "When I said that 'the most obvious persons who represented the SDS were Srdjo Srdic and Simo Miskovic,' I meant to say that these two persons most often spoke on behalf of the SDS."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "The reason for this was that these two persons held in succession the position of president of the SDS in Prijedor municipality."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "I do not remember which one of them was president of SDS first and which one later. I would also like to point out that while it was the SDS who called the shots, its plan was implemented in reality by one of its main leaders Milomir Stakic acting in his position as president of the illegal Prijedor Serb Municipal Assembly and as president of the municipal Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "Although I did not myself see any documents issued by the Crisis Staff, I heard and learned from others that Crisis Staff decided on all important matters."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "Crisis Staff was in charge of everything that happened in the municipality."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "May and June 1992, before I was prevented from working any longer, I learned, including from colleagues and media such as Radio Prijedor and Kozarski Vjesnik, et cetera, that all matters concerning employment, police, administrative services, and the war in the municipality were being controlled by the Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "I remember Stakic appearing in the media, acting as the president of the Crisis Staff, but I cannot recall when and in what specific situations this happened."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "Stakic's position as the president of the Crisis Staff was a well-known fact, and it was not something that would make me take any special notice."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "However, from having seen Stakic in the media, I concluded that he was very proud of his position and his role, and felt that he was doing the 'right' thing and that he was destined to do it."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure about "destined." But on the whole, yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "By doing the 'right' thing, I mean that he was in full agreement with the policies that he was implementing."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "I do not remember any specific instances in this regard, but I saw Stakic on TV, speaking as president of the Crisis Staff and read about him in the press, and that is the impression I was left with.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you go into some detail when you remember Stakic speaking on the TV as president of the Crisis Staff? What was this about? Do you remember this, by chance?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to remember now. That was a long time ago. I'm sorry, but I don't think I could say anything very specific. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you remember him acting as the president of the Crisis Staff and speaking in this capacity on television. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Proceed. "Stakic implemented the SDS plan, which was to ethnically cleanse the Prijedor municipality."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "I believe that the SDS had its aim the creation of a unified Serb state which would include parts of territories of Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia, and Montenegro."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the parts. I can't remember now, but I was talking about a unified Serb state with parts of Croat, Muslim -- this is not quite clear to me that I could have -- the phrasing strikes me as strange. I'm not sure if it's something in the translation, but the aim was to create Greater Serbia and not a state with parts of these regions and territories included. So this is unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's the purpose of today's exercise, to get it clarified and to understand what you really wanted to express and what you wanted to make part of today's hearing, your testimony.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember having said anything like that precisely, that the aim was to create a state including parts of Croatia and Muslim, Montenegrin. This is a clumsy phrase, or maybe a mistranslation, but I don't think I ever said anything quite like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you say anything about the creation of a unified Serb state?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have the impression, and based on what facts, that you may have said: "I believe that the SDS had its aim the creation of a unified Serb state."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can say that. But that phrase "with parts of Croatia" or something Muslim, I can't remember having said that. But the unified Serb state, yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore my question: What do you understand and what was your assessment in 1992 what would form the unified Serb state?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This unified Serb state would include parts of Croatia, maybe that's what the phrasing was about. The part of Croatia usually referred to as the Serbian Krajina, bordering near Knin and Bosnia-Herzegovina and then all the way to Slavonija, what was referred to as the Serbian Krajina. Parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, most of those parts that were Serb-controlled. Maybe that was what caused the confusion, and then Montenegro would have been included, too. But this refers to parts of Croatia, so I think it must have been a mistranslation after all. This Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. unified Serb state would have been composed of parts of Croatia, parts of Bosnia, and parts of Montenegro. Those parts of Bosnia where Serbs were predominant and those parts of Bosnia that they had taken militarily. I hope I have made this clear enough now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. You added then, and I continue the last line of page 3 of the statement from 2002: "The SDS plan implemented through Milomir Stakic acting in his capacity of president of Crisis Staff was to remove all or most non-Serbs from the territory of Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "Removal of non-Serbs was accomplished through several means including denial of employment, harassment, beatings, the detention of Muslim men and even women in camps, rapes, burnings of the houses and large-scale killings, both in and out of the detention camps."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "These actions all together created a physically and psychological environment which non-Serbs themselves became desperate to leave."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Judge Fassi Fihri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us you would have to expatriate yourself. You were forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you come back to Prijedor later?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did return in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you still there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I live there when I don't work, and I work in Sanski Most which means I spend weekends and afternoons there. I have two places of residence. I spend the morning and early afternoon in Sanski Most where I work at the health centre, and after work and on the weekends, I'm at home in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your family lives in Prijedor, too?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife and I live together, and my children are in (redacted) for education. I have two sons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your domicile nowadays is in Prijedor, your house, your family house?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You told us that Dr. Stakic was a gentleman.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Do you still have this opinion, appraisal? Do you still think that he's a respectable man, a gentleman?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say this, but in the context of selecting a candidate as a representative of the Serbian people for the position of the vice-president of the municipality. So maybe this is the context you were referring to when you used the word "gentleman." I meant -- what I meant is to have in such a position a man with a university degree, a well-respected person. If that's what you were referring to, yes, indeed, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification in the meantime, I asked the registry to redact from the transcript the country where our witness lives today. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Beglerbegovic, yesterday you testified transcript page 78, English version, the last lines of the page 7 and the first lines of the page 8: "At the time of the campaign for the founding of new parties, radical or liberal or a combination of these two parties -- I can't remember -- were created. But the president of that party was the man named Guberina. And the head of the party for this area of Omarska was then Mr. Stakic." And today, you also mentioned Guberina as a very famous person in the former Yugoslavia, a lawyer. Can you dwell upon in detail about this party, about the person of Guberina and the role of Dr. Stakic in the creation of this radical party?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there isn't much I can say about that party. I'm not even sure what its exact name was. When I said that the person at the head of the party was someone called Guberina, I was not aware at the time that this was the eminent Belgrade lawyer Guberina. I only heard that here in the courtroom from the Defence. I knew it was a man called Guberina. As far as I can remember, from what the people who attended the rally said, the party platform was a nationalist one because I know a man who told me that he was upset by certain things that Mr. Guberina said at the rally. And the man who told me this is a democrat, and he does not agree with a nationalist platform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what particularly Mr. Guberina said that was -- that upset your friend?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what it was exactly, but I do know that his reaction was such that he switched on his chainsaw so as to make a noise to drown out the voice of this Guberina. He was so irritated. But I don't know what the details were and what it was that prompted some of those present to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the relation of Dr. Stakic in regard of the founding of this party and the activity of this party, and especially the leader?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know what the connection was or how it came about that he was at the head of that party in the area of Prijedor. These are matters of which I know nothing, and somebody else might be able to clarify this for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Then Mr. Beglerbegovic, you said that the most obvious persons who represented the SDS were Srdjo Srdic and Simo Miskovic. It's page 3 of your testimony in January this year. Then how can you explain why Dr. Stakic, not Srdjo Srdic or Simo Miskovic, were elected vice-president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly before the takeover and president of the Crisis Staff after the takeover, and then the president of Municipal Assembly of Prijedor in 1996 again?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that yesterday. Dr. Stakic was from Omarska, or rather the villages from the Omarska area. This covers a large part of the Prijedor municipality inhabited purely by Serbs. And this area in all political negotiations had a right to have its own representative in the government. I think that this is why it was not Srdjo Srdic or Simo Miskovic who lived in the Prijedor, while Dr. Stakic actually came from that area. In these talks, they insisted that their be a representative from the area of Omarska, at least that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, as we have only little evidence on the personality of Dr. Stakic, could you please try to tell the Tribunal what was your assessment, what kind of person was Dr. Stakic, a more calm person? An energetic person. Please use your own words. How would you describe Dr. Stakic in the time you met him. And were there any changes, and please tell us then the exact time.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had few contacts with Dr. Stakic, so I'm not in a position to describe his personality. I met him on two occasions. One before the war when, as a young colleague, a doctor, he would come to my surgery. I was already a specialist. He came from Omarska and introduced himself. He was seeking an intervention for a relative of his. This relative wanted to retire early probably and needed a specialist to examine him. And he said that he had heard many nice things about me in Omarska and in his village and that it was his ambition to achieve the same sort of career that I had achieved, working in Omarska. After that, I don't know if we met very often, but we were on friendly terms. He always treated me very politely, very pleasantly, and I had the impression that this was a decent person. After that, the events that we have talked about here took place, and I was a little surprised to see what position he was in at the time, because I didn't know much about his political activities. And the meeting I had with him in 1996 was such that he actually didn't look at me. He was frowning. He was arrogant. He didn't look me in the eye. He was evasive. He ignored me. It's very hard to describe his character because I had few contacts with him apart from what I have just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I think your testimony can't be finalised without asking you another question, paraphrasing that what you said yesterday, one got the impression, and I believe you yourself made use of the notion of privilege, looking now back to the period of time in 1992, did you find out any reason why you opposed to so many other persons in Prijedor got this treatment one could regard, without being cynical, as a privileged treatment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the real reason, but probably I had worked in Omarska for ten years before the war and had contact with people, with patients and their families. And it was probably this that prompted the people who were either guards or at higher-ranking positions to respect me. And that's probably why I got the treatment I did. But I never really found out, and I don't know today, who it was that actually made the decision that I should be released. Nobody ever told me this, and I don't know. But that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have the impression that you had a kind Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of guardian angel in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I don't know about something like this. I can't think of any specific person who might have been my guardian angel. Perhaps it was God. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. It's only fair to ask the parties whether there were any additional questions right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, after your reading from the statement of the witness, we would probably need the whole day for the cross-examination of this witness again because you opened many questions which were not part of examination-in-chief. So I think -- I really don't know what to say now, but I think that we'll need another cross-examination. Our complete strategy of cross-examination of this witness would be completely different if we knew that this would be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence was aware of the statement. We all had before us, and you yourself quoted a paragraph that was part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did, but only that which was part of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please feel free to add questions if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we at least have a break so I have half an hour to prepare another set of questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First, the other way around, that you also can include possible other questions put forward by the OTP. Let's ask first the OTP, do you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then the trial stands adjourned until 5.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Defence counsel, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Beglerbegovic, I promised to no longer maltreat you with questions, but it seems that we must continue and socialise in this way for some more time. Would you please be so kind and muster up some more strength.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ask away, but don't maltreat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try not to. We shall have to analyse the part of your statement that His Honour Schomburg read out to you. So the same way as he did, I will just go sentence by sentence.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please have a translation of that statement in front of me because when sentences are read out like that, one by one, it can become very confusing. It gives only partial understanding, and it's very difficult to follow so that's why I would really like to have one, if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we can't see the page numbers in the B/C/S version, it's on top of the page, can you please turn to page number -- last three numbers 4525. His Honour Schomburg started out with the sixth paragraph on that page. The first sentence which reads: "I want to emphasise that after the takeover, there was no conflict between the president of the municipality and the SDS." You have already explained this and said that, in fact, you didn't know whether there was a conflict or not, nor were you in a position to know, considering the overall situation in Prijedor at that time. Can we therefore conclude that you did not know and do not know now whether there was a conflict at that time between Dr. Stakic and the president of the municipal board of the SDS of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence precisely demonstrates what creates all the confusion when you read out sentence by sentence. When you read the sentence, I want to emphasise that there was no conflict between the president of the municipality and the SDS after the takeover, if you take it out of the context, it can be questioned. But if you then follow up with they acted as one, then it's clear, and he did, in his capacity, carry out the SDS plan. Honestly, I never knew of any conflicts within the SDS. That's what I also stated in my first statement. I didn't know of any conflicts, but from what I can tell and from what was happening, that was not the impression I had. I had the impression that all was functioning well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that Mr. Miskovic was a powerful figure within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the party and its work, I think he was. Gradually, I think he became less prominent. But at the time when he was president of the party, yes, he was a very powerful man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you have said that you knew that Dr. Stakic had been replaced, believe me, I too, forgot the name of the man who replaced him.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kurnoga.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. So Mr. Kurnoga replaced Mr. Stakic in the position of president of the Municipal Assembly in the autumn of 1992. Does this show that there was a faction within the SDS that was powerful enough to replace the president of the municipality before his mandate expired?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the circumstances in which he was replaced. I'm not sure about any factions. I only know that a man was replaced, Stakic was no longer there, and Kurnoga came along. What the circumstances were or who was involved, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next paragraph, the one about Srdic and Miskovic, I will make no further comments on that because there is nothing to be commented on in that passage, at least I think so. However, I would like to ask some clarifications in connection with paragraph number 8. "I also want to point out that while the SDS was in power, plans, party plans on the ground were carried out by one of the leaders, Milomir Stakic who held the capacity of the president of the illegal Municipal Assembly of Prijedor and the municipal Crisis Staff." Do you know that even if he was the president of the Crisis Staff and the Municipal Assembly, did he have the real power or was the real actual power in the hands of people who were in the background? Can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about any people in the background. But it was logical to expect that if someone was at the head of the municipality, which is executive power, so that's also how he came to be the head of the Crisis Staff. It was to be expected, and as far as you are asking me whether I can provide an answer or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Stakic was not even invited to SDS meetings?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph, that is, the last paragraph on this page, you say that you never seen the documents issued by the Crisis Staff. That's the first sentence. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor took over the powers of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly because it was unable to meet?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's happened and that it was precisely because of this circumstance and others that the Crisis Staff was established, and it had the same role as the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the powers of the Municipal Assembly were on the one hand and the president of the Municipal Assembly on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I'm not all that familiar with it. I could speculate, but I wouldn't really know. It's something that is prescribed by law, but it would be difficult for me to interpret. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there any possibility, although you have told us you don't know, so I will not insist on this, but let me just put one additional question about this: Would it be possible for the Municipal Assembly or the Crisis Staff to command the army?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in the prevailing circumstances, when there was a state of chaos, it would be possible, although I would not be able to assert that because the people in power, the people in the government, and the people in the army were very close. Maybe they could not formally, legally issue a document ordering the army to do something, but I think that it was possible for them to influence the decisions that were made both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was possible for them to influence each other, but can you tell me whether you know if they were able to issue orders to each other?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be hard for me to assert this categorically because I was not in a position to know that. I think I have been clear enough about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you know how decisions were reached within the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Crisis Staff had any other powers apart from the powers of the Municipal Assembly, whose powers it explicitly took over?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly was established?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Dr. Stakic appeared in the media for the first time as the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will put only one further question, with the leave of the Court, which calls for conclusions by the witness. I will put the question, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. leave it to the Court to decide whether the witness should answer or not. The question would be as follows: Had you known about the conflicts within the SDS and the conflicts about the SDS policy, would that have changed your attitude or your opinion that it was Milomir Stakic who was implementing the policy of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My objection to the question is that it indicates a fact that there's no proof of, that there were conflicts within the SDS. The question is "had you known about conflicts within the SDS."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. Beglerbegovic, once again. I hope I will not question you again. Thank you. [In English] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then it's up to us to thank you very much for coming here, for giving us these answers for two days, and we wish you a good trip home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the parties can in the meantime prepare the continuing work on list 2, please. Apparently the OTP has...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. We should make a clear distinction now. It's now only on the question of the admission of evidence or into evidence, and not on the question of signatures. We'll come to this, back to this later. Yesterday, we had before us Exhibit Number 54. This is list 2. And we proceeded until the 65 ter number 257, which was admitted into evidence as S81. May we now come to the former document 267, provisional 82. This is called "Announcement on the Cancellation of Job Openings."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a little bit difficult. I wonder whether or not we should have at least in B/C/S two different numbers, because on the one hand side, we have this alleged piece of the newspaper, and then in addition, the document that reads at the end with number 997. So my proposal would be to have this piece from the newspaper as 82B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could mark it /1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
